content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on the use of long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) for HIV prevention. This review was conducted by a team of experts, including Lara Lorenzetti, Nhi Dinh, Ariane van der Straten, Virginia Fonner, Kathleen Ridgeway, Michelle Rodolph, Robin Schaefer, and Rachel Baggaley. Recent randomized trials have demonstrated the efficacy of CAB-LA as a long-acting injectable PrEP option. While CAB-LA offers significant benefits as an additional prevention method for populations at substantial risk of HIV, understanding community responses to injectable PrEP is essential before formal recommendations are made. The objective of this review was to systematically assess the values, preferences, and acceptability of injectable PrEP among end-users and community members to inform clinical guidance and global policy. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and complemented a separate review and meta-analysis on the safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness of CAB-LA as PrEP. A two-stage review process was used to evaluate references against eligibility criteria. Data from the included studies were organized based on constructs of acceptability, such as affective attitude, burden, ethicality, intervention coherence, opportunity costs, perceived effectiveness, and self-efficacy. The review identified 99 articles that met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 38 underwent rapid data extraction, while 61 were analyzed in greater detail using the acceptability framework. Most studies were observational, cross-sectional, or qualitative in design. Over half of the studies were conducted in North America, with men who have sex with men (MSM) being the most frequently studied population. While many studies examined injectable PrEP in general, including hypothetical or placebo products, six studies specifically focused on CAB-LA. Findings revealed an overall interest in and preference for injectable PrEP, though preferences varied across groups and regions. Injectable PrEP was seen as a potential solution to adherence challenges associated with daily or on-demand oral PrEP regimens. It was also considered a better fit for individuals seeking privacy, discretion, and less frequent dosing. However, concerns were raised about fear of needles, pain at the injection site, logistical challenges with attending regular appointments, and the possibility of waning or incomplete protection. The review concluded that injectable PrEP, including CAB-LA, should be included as part of a broader menu of HIV prevention options, given the overall interest and preference for this method. However, preferences for injectable PrEP may evolve over time. Future research is needed to explore how preferences change as more end-users gain experience with antiretroviral-containing injectables, rather than hypothetical or placebo products.
